title: Start with a real problem
subtitle: Replace an impressive-sounding product idea with an observable situation.
concept: Before building, identify who faces what difficulty, when it occurs, and what should improve.
intuition: If a friend asks for something tasty, you ask who is eating, where and with what constraints. Software needs that context too.
objectives: Describe one user, one moment and one specific difficulty.
State an observable sign that the problem has improved.

body.title: Start with a small inconvenience
body.text: Lin wants to study each evening but forgets yesterday's plan. The user is Lin; the moment is the start of study; the problem is plans buried in chats. Describe that before choosing buttons or technology. Wanting a cool website does not explain its purpose.

body.title: Describe actions, not feature names
body.text: Turn list management into actions: enter a plan and add it; mark it complete; delete it when no longer needed. These actions suggest a simple page. You need not know the code yet, but each action needs a purpose.

body.title: Give the agent a checkable starting point
body.text: Ask the agent to identify missing information, while choosing the intended user yourself. Whether plans survive refresh matters here. Whether to add particle effects does not solve the missing-plan problem.

formalDefinition.text: Before building, identify who faces what difficulty, when it occurs, and what should improve.
conditions: For small personal learning projects. In shared repositories, follow the team's conventions.
This method produces checkable evidence; it cannot guarantee arbitrary AI output is correct.

workflow: Describe one user, one moment and one specific difficulty.
List the actions needed to achieve the user's goal.
State an observable sign that the problem has improved.

workedExamples.title: From wish to scenario
workedExamples.problem: Rewrite: Build me an amazing learning tool.
steps: Choose yourself rather than every learner.
Identify difficulty finding plans before studying each day.
Define success as seeing unfinished plans on opening the page.
workedExamples.answer: Before studying each day, I want to find yesterday's plans. Build a study-list page where I can add plans, mark them complete and delete unwanted ones. Initially, only I will use it in my own browser.

workedExamples.title: Find missing requirements
workedExamples.problem: A friend wants a class-wide study list. Can you build it exactly like a personal list?
steps: Shared use means multiple readers and writers.
Ask whether lists are separate and whether people may edit others' items.
Agree on scope before discussing accounts and servers.
workedExamples.answer: Ask whether everyone shares one list, who may edit, and whether cross-device synchronization is required. These answers change the architecture; personal browser storage is not shared storage.

commonMistakes.correction: A framework describes implementation, not the actions a user needs.

commonMistakes.claim: AI should infer my real intention.
commonMistakes.correction: Have it state assumptions and questions. Confirm answers that would change the project's direction.

practice.problem: Rewrite: I want a productivity tool, as a use scenario.
practice.hint: Add a user, moment and difficulty.
practice.answer: After dinner, I waste time searching chats for study plans. I want one page showing unfinished items.
solution: Describe current behavior and friction instead of using efficient as a substitute for an observable change.

practice.problem: Is use React a user problem or an implementation choice?
practice.hint: A user can describe the goal without knowing a framework.
practice.answer: An implementation choice. A user problem might be plans disappearing after refresh.
solution: Separate the goal from the method.
Specify persistence before discussing how to implement it.

practice.problem: What is missing from a shared-list request?
practice.hint: Consider who may see and edit data.
practice.answer: Whether it is one shared list, who has editing rights, and whether synchronization and login are needed.
solution: List questions affecting permissions and data location.
Decide about a server after confirming the answers.

practice.problem: Give the simplest observable success for this example.
practice.hint: Use one action and one visible result.
practice.answer: After adding Practice Git, it appears in the list and can be found next time.
solution: The action is adding a plan.
The result is seeing and finding it again; later lessons specify persistence conditions.

learningCheck.question: Which statement is most useful before coding?
choices: Let me find unfinished plans each day
Use the most advanced technology stack
feedback: No concrete scenario makes completion hard to judge.
The user goal can now be broken into actions.
Technology still does not explain the problem.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Would you accept an agent's immediate suggestion of a leaderboard?

steps.question: The agent proposes building a leaderboard first. How do you respond?
choices: Ask how it helps me find my plans
feedback: This shifts the first release toward a different problem.
Relate the suggestion to the user goal before deciding.
Scope grows and verification becomes harder.

steps.question: The agent asks whether plans should survive refresh. What do you choose?
feedback: Finding tomorrow's plans depends on saving; answer explicitly.
Appearance does not answer the storage question.

steps.question: Which material is most useful to retain now?
choices: The user scenario and three essential actions
feedback: Rankings do not establish whether the user problem is solved.
These anchor scope and acceptance criteria.
Record future ideas separately so they do not obscure the first release.

interactiveVisual.followUp: Choose a real difficulty of your own. Describe its user, timing, actions and outcome.
